title: Electrically tunable, two-photon interference from remote silicon-vacancy centers in industrial silicon carbide
authors: Fedor Dzmitryevich Hrunski, Daniel Scheller, Maximilian Hollendonner, Kim Ullerich, Shravan Kumar Parthasarathy, Chiun Fu, Andre Pointner, Wolfgang Knolle, Florian Kaiser, Durga Bhaktavatsala Rao Dasari, Roland Nagy
abstract: Distributed quantum networks rely on spatially separated, independently operated quantum systems as network nodes, whose emitted photons must be interfered with high visibility to establish end-to-end entanglement. Crucially, for network-relevant applications, high visibilities must be achieved over prolonged timescales to reduce overheads for error correction, and to increase network rates. Here, we demonstrate experimentally that silicon vacancy $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ color centers in silicon carbide (SiC) achieve these requirements, notably in a mass-deployable fashion. We integrate $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers in different industrial-grade SiC p-i-n diodes, which are controlled via voltage biassing. This way, we demonstrate both, spectral overlapping of 19 randomly selected $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers in different diodes, as well as spectral narrowing close to the lifetime limit, i.e., typically below 60 MHz. Notably, these performance parameters are long-term stable, e.g., readjusting the p-i-n diode bias is required only every 8.4 hours, which reduces significantly the overall experimental overhead. We then use these assets to demonstrate high-quality two-photon interference between $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers located in two different cryostat setups, which are spatially separated by two meters. Notably, we perform a 26-days long measurement campaign, demonstrating two-photon interference with state-of-the-art raw interference visibilities of 82%, which aligns with the current state-of-the-art. These results establish $\mathrm{V_{Si}}$ centers in industry-grade SiC devices as a scalable, spectrally stable building block for distributed quantum networks.
summary: This paper demonstrates the feasibility of using silicon vacancy (V_Si) centers in industrial silicon carbide (SiC) as robust quantum network nodes. By electrically tuning and stabilizing the emission frequency, the researchers achieved high-visibility two-photon interference over a 26-day period between two spatially separated sources. These results establish V_Si in SiC as a scalable and stable building block for quantum communication.
main_problem: The core challenge is demonstrating high-visibility, long-term stable two-photon interference from spatially separated quantum nodes for use in distributed quantum networks.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated two-photon interference with a raw visibility of 82% over a 26-day measurement campaign using VSi centers in industrial SiC devices.
method: The experiment utilized two-photon interference (HOM) measurements between two remote quantum emitters, combined with electrical biasing to achieve spectral tuning and stability.
model_or_system: The platform consists of silicon vacancy (V_Si) color centers embedded in industrial-grade silicon carbide (SiC) p-i-n diodes. These centers are electrically controlled via voltage biasing, allowing for spectral tuning and maintaining coherence over long periods.
key_observables: Two-photon interference visibility (raw visibility of 82%), spectral linewidths (narrowed below 60 MHz), and long-term stability (requiring bias adjustment every 8.4 hours).
important_parameters: Two-meter separation distance, 26-day measurement duration, and the achievable spectral narrowing limit (e.g., 29.62 MHz).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that the measured visibility is limited by the intrinsic properties of the VSi centers in the SiC matrix, which are shown to be scalable.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup with two samples in separate cryostats, the dependence of the A2 transition frequency on reverse bias, and the characterization of multiple VSi centers across different diodes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical platform (V_Si in SiC p-i-n diodes) to demonstrating spectral control (tuning and narrowing) and culminates in the long-term, high-visibility two-photon interference measurement between remote nodes.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, scalable solid-state implementation for quantum networking nodes, directly addressing the critical engineering hurdles of spectral stability and long-term coherence required for quantum repeaters.
